text: A switch and a router both move traffic, but they make completely different decisions. A switch forwards based on Layer 2 MAC addresses and learns its MAC address table by watching traffic go by. A router forwards based on Layer 3 IP addresses, using a routing table it learns dynamically or has configured by hand. This lesson walks through both, plus the actual hop-by-hop path a packet takes between them.

The first time a switch sees a frame addressed to an unknown MAC, it doesn't know which port leads there, so it floods that frame out every port except the one it arrived on. Whichever device owns that address replies, and the switch records the source MAC and port from that reply. From then on, frames to that address go out exactly one port — this show mac address-table output is exactly that learned map.

Here's the actual path. Host A checks whether the destination is on its own subnet. If not, it sends the frame to its default gateway instead. The switch forwards that frame by MAC address alone, straight to the router's port. The router reads the destination IP, checks its routing table, and rebuilds a brand-new frame with new MAC addresses before sending it on to Host B.

A router matches a packet's destination IP against its routing table and picks the most specific matching entry — the longest prefix match. A directly connected slash-24 network wins over a broader match, and if nothing specific fits, the default route, written as zero-zero-zero-zero slash zero, catches everything else and sends it toward the gateway of last resort.

A collision domain is the set of devices whose transmissions could collide — every switch port is its own collision domain today. A broadcast domain is different: it's everyone who receives a broadcast frame, and a switch floods broadcasts out every port, so it never shrinks a broadcast domain. Only a router actually breaks one into smaller pieces.

The one fact worth locking in: MAC addresses change at every hop, but the packet's source and destination IP addresses stay the same all the way from Host A to Host B. Next up, Lesson 7 covers DNS — how a name like a website address actually becomes one of those IP addresses in the first place.
